title: Arete 27B Workflow: Setup, Settings and Costs (2026)
summary: Arete 27b workflow setup starts with the vendor's baseline configuration. Find what blocks faster processing and solutions for each common issue.
body_markdown:
## Stage 1: Get Arete 27B Responding


Get one reply by obtaining the weights or a hosted endpoint, copying the exact model name from the vendor page, and sending a single prompt. Which file or GPU you choose decides whether that first call works.


### Get Arete 27B access or download GGUF weights


Before you download anything, know that the quantized files in[mradermacher's Arete-27B-GGUF repository](https://huggingface.co/mradermacher/Arete-27B-GGUF) are third-party conversions, not vendor releases. Their sizes are real, but they cover weights only:


- Q4_K_M is 16.6 GB
- Q5_K_M is 19.3 GB
- Q6_K is 22.2 GB
- Q8_0 is 28.7 GB
- BF16 is 53.81 GB


So Q4_K_M, Q5_K_M and Q6_K load on a 24 GB card. Q6_K leaves under 2 GB for context, so long prompts may fail to load. Q8_0 and BF16 don't fit on 24 GB, so skip them for a first run.


**Without a suitable GPU, rent one** .[RunPod's GPU list](https://www.runpod.io/gpu-models) shows the L40S at $0.79 per hour, enough to hold Q8_0, so practitioners can run model inference without major capital expense. The A100 PCIe 80GB is $1.19 per hour, and the H100 PCIe is $1.99.


Only those 80 GB cards hold BF16, so pay the extra $0.40 or $1.20 per hour only if you need full precision. These prices are for GPUs that fit any 27B model, not Arete specifically.


### Run Arete 27B locally with llama.cpp or Ollama


A GGUF file is served locally by llama.cpp or Ollama, and both expose an HTTP endpoint you can call like any hosted API.


With llama.cpp, start` llama-server` with the file path (or` -hf mradermacher/Arete-27B-GGUF:Q4_K_M` to pull it) and a context size no larger than the model card allows. It listens on port 8080 by default and answers OpenAI-style requests at` /v1/chat/completions` .


With Ollama,` ollama run hf.co/mradermacher/Arete-27B-GGUF:Q4_K_M` downloads and starts the model, and the server answers on port 11434. Its OpenAI-compatible route is` /v1/chat/completions` there too. Use the model name your runtime reports, and set the sampling values from the model card in the request body.


Your baseline script then posts to` http://localhost:8080/v1/chat/completions` or the Ollama equivalent, with one fixed prompt and the saved settings. The same URL and body go into the Activepieces HTTP step later.


A cloud-hosted Activepieces cannot reach` localhost` , so for a local model run Activepieces on the same network or expose the endpoint deliberately, with authentication.


### Enter the exact model name and endpoint


Copy the model identifier and base URL from the vendor's page, or from the repository name if you run the GGUF locally. A name that's one character off usually produces a "model not found" error, which **looks like an outage but is a typo** .


If the page gives no endpoint, write "not documented" and use the one your runtime prints at startup.


### Send a test prompt and confirm the reply


Send a short, fixed prompt such as "Reply with the single word: ready." Check three things: the call returned, the text isn't empty, and you can save it to a file. A fixed prompt gives you a baseline to compare against once you add steps.


**502 integrations sit in the connector library** of the no-code automation tool that later stages pass this call's output into, meaning data reaches most services in a typical business stack.


The plain HTTP integration in that library sends the same request you just made by hand.
